visible.summary:
Israel is the Middle East's most progressive destination for trans visitors, with no criminalisation, anti-discrimination protections, court-based legal gender recognition (with dead-name removal from IDs as of 2025), publicly funded transition healthcare, and Tel Aviv as a regional queer hub.

Two traveler-specific risks pull the score down. First, Ben-Gurion Airport has no regulations for interacting with trans travelers — documented humiliating questioning and detainment, with surgery demanded for gender recognition ("If you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male"). Every foreign visitor transits Ben-Gurion, making this a high-probability friction point. Second, violence is rising sharply: 433 homophobic/transphobic physical incidents were reported in 2025, including dating-app traps and organized ambushes, with transgender people "bearing the brunt." Trump's anti-trans rhetoric is reportedly inflaming the local climate.

The right-wing Netanyahu coalition and the Israel-Hamas war aftermath have weakened protections, though the National Security Committee has convened on LGBTQ public-space security.
visible.tangentialFactors: Dating-app traps and organized ambushes are a direct caution for trans visitors using apps.
visible.localsOnly: Court-based LGR with dead-name removal (2025) and publicly funded transition healthcare are resident-facing.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Security risks from the Israel-Hamas conflict (rockets, terrorism, border areas) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Haaretz: first-person account of a transgender traveller's ordeal at an Israeli airport — security insisting 'if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male', documenting gender-identity humiliation at border screening.
Jerusalem Post (2025 data): homophobic and transphobic violence rose in Israel during 2025 — official data showing an increase in anti-LGBTQ attacks.
Ynet: anti-LGBTQ violence hit a record high in Israel — dating-app traps and organised ambushes luring victims to attacks; record assault totals.
Haaretz: Trump's inflammatory rhetoric is affecting Israel's transgender community — US discourse spilling into local climate; trans Israelis report heightened fear.
Haaretz: Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people — protocol change after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees/travellers.
Jerusalem Post: registration of a person's previous name abolished for transgender people — document-change policy removing old-name traceability.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 404 - page removed); the underlying page addressed trans rights in Israel - laws, protections and gaps.

Outright International (last update 12 Mar 2026): Israel at-a-glance — no criminalization of consensual same-sex acts in the criminal code, some legal protections, but no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register; baseline legal matrix.

Times of Israel: 'Most Israelis favor same-sex marriage, but half of MKs mum on issue' - a Channel 10 survey found majority public support for same-sex marriage while half of lawmakers declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.

visible.summary:
Argentina has one of the world's most progressive legal frameworks — the 2012 Gender Identity Law allows administrative self-identification (no medical requirements), offers an X marker for non-binary people, and funds transition healthcare. Buenos Aires is "one of the safest major cities in Latin America for LGBTQ+ visitors."

But the situation is deteriorating sharply under the Milei government: the president has called "gender ideology" "child abuse," issued decrees modifying the Gender Identity Law, and hate crimes hit a record 227 in 2025 (up 62%, one every 38 hours — trans women bearing the brunt). Police institutional violence against trans and travesti women is documented (arbitrary raids, drug-law criminalisation, searches only on travestis). The violence targets local vulnerable communities rather than tourists, but the trajectory is concerning.

The 2012 self-ID law remains in force for adults and courts are pushing back on the Milei decrees.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010 (first in Latin America) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with a same-sex partner.
visible.localsOnly: The Milei decrees banning minors' hormone therapy and surgery, and the prison-housing decree, affect residents; the self-ID law, X marker and state-funded transition healthcare are domestic administrative processes a visitor does not use.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: General crime (robbery, scams) in Buenos Aires affects all tourists; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (Apr 10, 2025): interviews in Buenos Aires (Apr 4, 2025) with trans activists — including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán (stabbed to death 2015) and Lohana Berkins — saying President Milei's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence; the situation described as 'chaotic, desperate'.

Agencia Presentes (Mar 19, 2026): the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025 — a record year, averaging one every 38 hours, marking an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Agencia Presentes (Feb 6, 2025): President Milei's government issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it pertains to minors, plus another decree on housing of transgender people in prisons; legal experts call the decree illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2025) covers Argentina's decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors.

Outright International Argentina overview (updated Mar 12, 2026): Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality (2010) and passed one of the world's most progressive gender-identity laws in 2012 allowing legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval; anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws — while the page's at-a-glance panel reports current negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration under review.

misterb&b Buenos Aires safety guide (updated May 28, 2026): first-person account of walking Buenos Aires at every hour, giving practical gay-traveler safety impressions for the Argentine capital — commercial gay-travel guide, useful as a recent on-the-ground visitor perspective.

Wikipedia, Gender Identity Law (Argentina), Law 26,743: approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated 24 May 2012; lauded by the United Nations as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region; allows legal gender change without surgery or court approval.

Infobae (Apr 5, 2025): Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence for Gabriel Marino, convicted of the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020 — meaning the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied.

visible.summary:
The UAE is one of the most thoroughly documented trans-traveler-hostile countries in the world. At the border, trans visitors have been X-rayed to check their genitals (Israeli trans women, detained and denied entry at Dubai airport), deported for having a male passport (Thai model Rachaya Noppakaroon at Expo 2020; Gigi Gorgeous), denied entry despite valid UAE visas (Indian trans person), and sentenced to prison for "dressing in a feminine way" (Singaporean trans woman, 1 year in Abu Dhabi). A Brazilian trans woman was arrested in her Dubai apartment by plainclothes police accusing her of drug trafficking.

The state "employs various legal mechanisms to explicitly acknowledge and penalize nonconformity with traditional gender roles" and actively targets "non-Emirati tourists." There is no legal gender recognition.

However, the UAE does not have the death penalty for same-sex conduct (unlike Saudi Arabia or Iran), no documented custodial death of a trans person (unlike Saudi), and some trans visitors do enter successfully if their passport gender matches their presentation. The targeting is triggered by passport/presentation mismatch, not blanket.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors travelling with a partner, or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Strict rules on social behaviour, drug possession, and financial crimes (exit bans) affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Ynetnews (2025): two Israeli trans women describe being detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched their female passport records, mocked by staff, and denied entry with passports confiscated — a direct visitor-experience account of gender-document screening at UAE entry.

VICE (Mar 21, 2022): Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon (2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up) was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand before her Expo 2020 appearance because her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

Metropoles (Apr 2023, Portuguese): a Brazilian trans woman detained in the UAE since September 2022 — arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test — accused the consulate of negligence; a documented case of a trans foreigner in prolonged UAE custody.

Cairo 52 legal review of the United Arab Emirates: the UAE employs various legal mechanisms that explicitly acknowledge and penalise nonconformity with traditional gender roles; transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion — the legal-framework basis for visitor risk.

Outright International UAE country overview (last updated Mar 12, 2026): a new federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment (Article 409 also covers unmarried different-sex couples); charges require a complaint basis; no legal gender recognition and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

TMZ (Aug 9, 2016): trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport, headlined as 'Dubai won't let me in because I'm transgender' — an early high-profile case of a trans visitor refused UAE entry on identity grounds.

visible.summary:
South Africa has one of the world's most progressive constitutional frameworks for trans rights — it was the first country to ban discrimination on sexual orientation (1996), has a legal gender recognition procedure (the Alteration of Sex Description Act, 2003), marriage equality (2006), and an Equality Act prohibiting unfair discrimination on gender. The Equality Court recently ruled in favour of a trans inmate who was denied gender expression and healthcare in prison (the Mokoena case, November 2025), affirming the constitutional right to gender-affirming healthcare for inmates, and Correctional Services has developed a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners.

But there is a wide gap between law and lived reality. LGR is administratively difficult, expensive, and inconsistently implemented ("the Mariana Trench of transphobia"). A trans woman was brutally attacked in a Tshwane tavern (January 2025); a Grindr-hostage ordeal was reported (December 2024); and anti-transgender violence has been documented within the public health system. There is a legal debate about whether businesses can refuse trans people facility access under the Consumer Protection Act.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, private healthcare available, and Cape Town and Johannesburg have established queer scenes. The violence targets local trans communities, not tourists.
visible.tangentialFactors: The Grindr-hostage ordeal (December 2024) is a caution for trans visitors using apps; the facility-access legal debate affects visitors' everyday exposure.
visible.localsOnly: The Alteration of Sex Description Act LGR procedure (difficult, expensive, inconsistently implemented) is resident-facing; the Mokoena prison case and the public-health-system violence concern residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: South Africa's high general crime rate (violent crime, carjackings, muggings) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: Full judgment, Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Gauteng High Court, delivered ~14 Nov 2025): refusal to provide gender-affirming health care to a transgender inmate for whom it was prescribed falls below the required standard of health care; refusal to allow feminising clothing/accessories likewise impugned — binding equality-court remedies for detained trans persons.

Lawyers for Human Rights case summary (14 Nov 2025): the High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services — orders DCS to implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs for transgender inmates, and provide prescribed medical care.

SAHRC media statement (14 Nov 2025): welcomes the Gauteng High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Case 2024/070075) under PEPUDA — orders compelling DCS to provide gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense and to permit clothing/cosmetics expressing her gender identity.

GroundUp (6 Aug 2025): Correctional Services has a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners but rights organisations doubt implementation; Lawyers for Human Rights represents a trans prisoner (NM) challenging conditions — pre-echo of the Nov 2025 Equality Court win.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): Civil Union Act in force 2006; since 2003 trans/intersex people can amend sex markers under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act (medical requirements pathologise identity; reform toward self-determination pending); 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; violence disproportionately hits black lesbian/trans/gender-nonconforming people in townships.

GroundUp opinion (27 Jun 2025, Mikhail Petersen): ordinary administrative tasks are fraught with risk for trans people — medical requirements under the Alteration Act lock people out of legal gender recognition, binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; Gender Dynamix's 2024 report documents a trans woman denied filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID (police mockery).

MambaOnline (6 Jan 2025): 23-year-old trans woman Aobakwe Mahlobo (make-up artist, Soshanguve→Winterveld) survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 Dec 2024, left with severe facial injuries and physical/emotional scars — she spoke out publicly; illustrates violent hate-crime risk against visible trans women in social venues.

OUT LGBT Well-being rights watch (Dec 2024): East London activists spotlighted trans healthcare access — memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long treatment delays; escalating hate violence with five LGBTQIA+ murders reported; also covers the Tshwane tavern attack (arrest made).

Academic article (PER/PELJ 2024) 'Did the CPA Shut the Bathroom Door?': analyses whether gender-segregated bathrooms to the exclusion of transgender/non-binary persons constitute unfair discrimination under CPA s9 read with Constitution s9 — argues trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access; relevant to visitor facility anxiety.

Daily Maverick opinion (19 Jan 2026, Mikhail Petersen/Gender Dynamix): makes the legal gender recognition case — mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and even arrest threats for 'fraud'; defines LGR as changing marker/name on official documents to align with identity; argues recognition should be a right grounded in dignity.

IOL/SAPA: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence, citing the Constitution's equality clause — early (2010s-era) government recognition of LGBTI violence as a policy problem; historic context for the later Hate Crimes Act (2024).

visible.summary:
Indonesia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — with a directly documented trans-traveler death in custody and a presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ as a national security threat. Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard trans activist from Peru, died in Bali police custody in 2022 after arrest at Bali airport on his honeymoon (family alleges police beating; police deny violence).

In Aceh province, Sharia law criminalises same-sex relations with public caning (applies to all persons in Aceh, including tourists). A new penal code effective January 2026 effectively criminalises all same-sex conduct nationally. President Prabowo in October 2025 classified "promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" as a national security threat alongside terrorism — and vigilante mob attacks on trans women escalated after this decree (10 attacks documented in Bogor between March and July 2026). Police conduct discriminatory raids on gay gatherings (75 arrested in Bogor in June 2025).

BUT: Bali is a major tourist hub where many trans visitors enter discreetly without incident; Indonesia has no death penalty; and Rodrigo's death is disputed (police deny violence) rather than clearly documented state torture.
visible.tangentialFactors: The new penal code (January 2026) criminalising all same-sex conduct nationally, and Aceh's Sharia caning provision (applying to tourists), are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Drug laws are severe (Rodrigo was arrested on drug charges); general terrorism/crime risks in certain regions affect all travellers.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2022) covers Indonesian police denying violence in the death of Harvard trans activist Rodrigo Ventocilla in Bali.

Harvard Crimson (Sept 2022): Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; on a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody, and his mother alleges police beat him — a documented death-in-custody case involving a trans traveler.

The Diplomat (14 August 2026, Robin Vochelet): vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law — President Prabowo Subianto's October 2025 presidential decree listing nonmilitary threats framed LGBTQ+ people within national defense policy. Article ties the violence and the official framing together as one escalation.

ABC News (15 August 2026): attacks on trans women 'did not suddenly appear' — analysis ties the surge to officials' latest verbal attacks and to the October 2025 presidential defense decree treating LGBT people as national-defense 'risks'. Academic commentator: the regulation shifts rhetoric 'into the official doctrine of national defence policy... risks that must be monitored and controlled'.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2025) covers Aceh province publicly caning two men for a same-sex relationship.

Outright International country page (updated 12 March 2026): Indonesia's new penal code took effect 2 January 2026 (signed December 2022) and penalises all consensual extra-marital sex between adults (reported as up to 2 years' imprisonment). Since same-sex marriage is not permitted, this effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations, with prosecution reported as selective — the current-law baseline for this record.
Human Dignity Trust country profile: two provinces of Indonesia (Aceh and South Sumatra) criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; national-level provisions target morality.

Amnesty International (June 2025): police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor on Sunday 22 June 2025, arresting 75 people (74 men, 1 woman) after public reports of a 'gay party'. Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena called it 'a blatant violation of human rights and privacy' and said the gathering violated no law — evidence of venue-based raids targeting LGBT gatherings near Jakarta.

HRW (7 July 2026) 'Indonesia: Surge in Abuse Against LGBT Students': HRW has documented discriminatory regulations, arrests and criminal trials against LGBT people in Indonesia since 2016, following officials' condemnations of a student group at Universitas Indonesia; Arus Pelangi, Indonesia's LGBT umbrella organization, documented 94 cases. Officials in early July called on parents to monitor children in 'this lifestyle'.

HRW report (10 August 2016) 'These Political Games Ruin Our Lives': the Indonesian Psychiatric Association proclaimed same-sex orientation and transgender identities 'mental illnesses' and recommended psychological 'rehabilitation', while the Jokowi government remained mostly silent — the origin point of the institutionalized anti-LGBT posture the record describes.

visible.summary:
Kenya is a dangerous destination for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the colonial-era Penal Code (14 years, applies to all including tourists). Police extortion targeting trans people is documented and systemic — a trans woman was forced to pay a $50 bribe in Mombasa, and 25 trans and intersex people told CNN this kind of police harassment is "common." The Kenya Human Rights Commission's "Lives on the Line" report documented 102 evictions, 43 unlawful arrests, and mob violence (groups stripping queer people naked) over a one-year period. An LGBTQ+ activist, Edwin Chiloba, was murdered (his body found in a metal box) — though the perpetrator was sentenced to 50 years, showing enforcement can work.

However, Kenya's courts have been a surprising bright spot. The High Court ruled in 2025 that a trans woman's arrest for "personation" was unconstitutional (awarding damages and ordering the government to draft a Transgender Protection Rights Bill). In May 2026, the High Court affirmed a constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Supreme Court has upheld LGBTQ+ freedom of association, and the Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional. "Thousands of gay travelers visit annually through specialized tour operators."

There is no anti-discrimination law and no LGR procedure yet, but the court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill is a positive trajectory.
visible.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, applies to tourists) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
visible.localsOnly: The court-ordered Transgender Protection Rights Bill and the 2026 LGR ruling are resident-facing developments; the eviction/arrest/mob-violence toll falls on residents.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism risks near the Somali border, general crime, and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Kenya (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

KHRC press release: Eldoret High Court handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

GATE.ngo on Nairobi Milimani High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026 (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of Jan 2020): follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a Kenyan man sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.
